_doc: Claims of KNOWN truth about the "shop" fixture, fed straight to the verifiers by `prr calibrate` to measure whether verification discriminates or rubber-stamps. 7 are false and 3 are true. A false claim must be PLAUSIBLE and refutable by reading or running the fixture's code — never by taste — because a false claim that gives itself away measures nothing; the true ones catch the opposite failure, a verifier that refutes everything. `truth` and `why` are the answer key and never reach any agent (`prr calibrate` copies an allow-list of finding fields). Keep the two sets indistinguishable in tone, length and self_confidence: any field that correlates with truth is a shortcut a verifier can take instead of reading the code.

claims.title: A coupon worth more than the cart zeroes the order total and the goods ship free
claims.body: applyCoupon clamps the discount with Math.max(0, ...), so a coupon whose amount exceeds the cart total produces 0 instead of the coupon being rejected or capped at what is owed. placeOrder stores that 0 as the order total, so the order is recorded as fully paid at nothing while the items are still on it. The clamp hides the condition rather than surfacing it.
claims.scenario: Cart of 30, coupon { minSpend: 10, amount: 50 }: applyCoupon(30, coupon) returns 0, and placeOrder writes an order with total 0 whose items list 30 of goods.
claims.evidence: src/cart.js:13 clamps the difference at 0; src/cart.js:12 checks only total against coupon.minSpend, never coupon.amount against total; src/orders.js:5 stores the returned total verbatim; no caller re-checks it.
claims.why: FALSE: real behaviour, not introduced by this change. `git show main:src/cart.js` line 14 is byte-identical to line 13 here; the commit touches applyCoupon only on line 12 (>= became >), the opposite boundary. A verifier that reads the base version caps it as pre-existing; one that reads only the new file confirms it.

claims.title: averageItemPrice returns NaN for an empty cart instead of 0
claims.body: The empty-cart guard that stood at the top of averageItemPrice is gone, so an empty cart reaches the division with both operands 0 and the function returns NaN. NaN then travels into whatever formats or compares the average and fails every comparison silently, so the caller sees no error, only a wrong number. README.md:6 states that this function returns 0 for an empty cart.
claims.scenario: averageItemPrice([]): cartTotal([]) is 0 and count is 0, so 0 / 0 evaluates to NaN. The existing test at test/cart.test.js:8-9 asserts 0 and now fails.
claims.evidence: src/cart.js:5-7 has no length check; `git show main:src/cart.js` line 6 held `if (!items.length) return 0`; README.md:6 documents the 0; test/cart.test.js:9 asserts it.
claims.why: TRUE: the `nan-empty-cart` defect of evals/fixtures/shop/expected.json. The diff for src/cart.js deletes the guard, and `node --test` in the checkout fails at test/cart.test.js:9 with `NaN !== 0`.

claims.title: formatLineItem throws a TypeError on an item that has no name
claims.body: formatLineItem dereferences item.name with no check that the property is there. Cart items are built by callers and nothing in this module requires a name: cartTotal and placeOrder both accept items carrying only price and qty, and the new test builds exactly such an item. One nameless item in a cart therefore throws instead of costing the receipt a line.
claims.scenario: receiptLines([{ price: 10, qty: 1 }]): item.name is undefined, undefined.trim() throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'trim')`, and the caller gets no receipt at all.
claims.evidence: src/cart.js:19 dereferences item.name unguarded; test/orders.test.js:6 builds an item with no name; src/cart.js:2 shows the module treating name as optional.
claims.why: FALSE: the fixture's bait (`bait-null-name` in expected.json). formatLineItem is module-private (src/cart.js:18 has no export) and its only caller is receiptLines, which filters to `item && typeof item.name === 'string'` on src/cart.js:23 before mapping, so line 19 can only ever see a string. In the checkout, `node -e "import('./src/cart.js').then(m=>console.log(m.receiptLines([{price:10,qty:1}])))"` prints `[]`.

claims.title: receiptLines can lose a paid line when the cart is mutated while it runs
claims.body: receiptLines walks items twice, once to filter and once to map. Carts are shared mutable arrays and placeOrder keeps a reference to the very same array while it awaits its insert, so an async task that splices items between the two passes leaves the receipt disagreeing with what was charged. The helper should take its own snapshot once.
claims.scenario: A handler calls receiptLines(cart.items) while an in-flight placeOrder resumes after `await db.insert` and removes an out-of-stock entry from that same array: the filter has already counted the item, the map runs over the shortened array, and the receipt is a line short.
claims.evidence: src/cart.js:23 chains filter and map over the caller's array; src/orders.js:5 puts that same array reference on the order; src/orders.js:7 yields the event loop inside placeOrder.
claims.why: FALSE: `items.filter(...).map(...)` on src/cart.js:23 is one synchronous expression containing no await, and JavaScript runs a task to completion, so nothing can interleave between the two passes. map also runs over the new array filter returned, so a later mutation of items cannot reach it. There is no concurrency here to exploit.

claims.title: Item names written by placeOrder are interpolated unescaped into the customer lookup query
claims.body: placeOrder writes the whole items array, caller-supplied name strings included, into the orders row without escaping or validating any of it. The lookup this commit adds builds its statement by string interpolation, so that stored text comes back out through the query: a name carrying a single quote closes the literal and the rest of it is parsed as SQL. Storing raw text is only safe while every reader parameterises, and this reader does not.
claims.scenario: An order is placed with items [{ name: "Mug'; DROP TABLE orders;--", price: 10, qty: 1 }]; the row is written on src/orders.js:7, and the next lookup splices that stored text into the statement on src/orders.js:15.
claims.evidence: src/orders.js:7 inserts the order built on line 5 out of the caller's items; src/orders.js:15 builds its statement with a template literal; nothing between the two escapes or validates.
claims.why: FALSE: the data path does not exist. src/orders.js:15 interpolates exactly one value, its own customerName parameter; stored item names are never re-interpolated, since the query only matches customer_name and returns rows. db.insert('orders', order) is handed a structured object, not SQL. That line is genuinely injectable (shop-06) but not by this route, so confirming this claim means the verifier matched on "SQL plus interpolation" instead of following the value.

claims.anchor: const rows = await db.query(`SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_name = '${customerName}' ORDER BY created_at DESC`)
claims.title: customerName is interpolated straight into the orders lookup SQL
claims.body: findOrdersByCustomer builds its statement with a template literal and drops customerName inside the quotes. The parameter is a plain string handed in by the caller, so a quote in it ends the literal and the remainder of the value is parsed as SQL. Any call site that passes a search field through hands over the orders table. The statement has to be parameterised.
claims.scenario: findOrdersByCustomer(db, "x' OR '1'='1") produces `... WHERE customer_name = 'x' OR '1'='1' ORDER BY created_at DESC`, returning every customer's orders; `x'; DROP TABLE orders;--` ends the statement outright.
claims.evidence: src/orders.js:15 interpolates ${customerName} into the statement text; the function is exported on src/orders.js:14 and validates nothing; there is no escaping or allow-list anywhere under src/.
claims.why: TRUE: the `sql-injection` defect of expected.json. The whole statement is built by the template literal on src/orders.js:15 with ${customerName} inside the quotes, and the function is new in this commit.

claims.title: The receipt drops items that the order was charged for
claims.body: placeOrder stores and returns every item it was given, while the receipt helper added in the same commit keeps only items whose name is a string. The two now describe one purchase differently: the customer pays for an item that never appears on their receipt, and anyone reconciling a receipt against the stored order finds a line missing with nothing recording why it went.
claims.scenario: placeOrder(db, { id: 1 }, [{ name: 'Mug', price: 10, qty: 1 }, { price: 5, qty: 1 }], null) charges 15 and hands its items to receiptLines on the way out, which keeps only the named one: the stored order and the receipt it returns disagree, and the customer is billed for a line their receipt never shows.
claims.evidence: src/orders.js:5-11 builds the order from the unfiltered items and returns it through the receipt helper added in the same commit; src/cart.js:23 keeps only items whose name is a string; src/cart.js:2 charges for every item whatever its name.
claims.why: FALSE on its mechanism: placeOrder never calls receiptLines. src/orders.js:1 imports only cartTotal and applyCoupon, placeOrder returns { ok, order } with no receipt in it, and `grep -rn receiptLines` in the checkout finds a single hit — the definition at src/cart.js:22. The scenario asserts a hand-off that does not exist, so it is refutable by reading src/orders.js rather than by arguing about impact.

claims.title: The empty-cart test passes whatever averageItemPrice returns
claims.body: assert.equal compares with ==, which coerces both sides first, so this assertion never pins the return value to 0 — it accepts anything that coerces to it. The one behaviour the test exists to protect, the empty-cart result documented in README.md:6, is left unprotected, and a change to averageItemPrice lands with the suite still green. It has to be assert.strictEqual.
claims.scenario: averageItemPrice([]) now evaluates 0 / 0; the test on test/cart.test.js:8-9 still reports ok, so nothing in the suite flags that the guard went.
claims.evidence: test/cart.test.js:9 calls assert.equal, not assert.strictEqual; src/cart.js:5-7 is the code it covers; README.md:6 states the expected 0.
claims.why: FALSE: refuted by the line above the anchor and by running the suite. test/cart.test.js:2 imports node:assert/strict, where equal IS strictEqual; loose == would not save it either, since NaN == 0 is false. `node --test` in the checkout fails at test/cart.test.js:9 with `Expected values to be strictly equal: NaN !== 0`, so the test does precisely what the claim says it cannot.

claims.title: The new placeOrder test cannot fail
claims.body: The test calls placeOrder, awaits it and ends. It asserts nothing: not that the insert happened, not which table it went to, not the total, not the shape that came back. It passes for any implementation that does not throw, including one that drops the order on the floor, so it buys a coverage point and protects nothing.
claims.scenario: Replace the body of placeOrder with `return { ok: true }` and delete the insert entirely: `node --test test/orders.test.js` still reports ok.
claims.evidence: test/orders.test.js:4-7 contains no assert call, and lines 1-2 import only node:test and placeOrder — node:assert is never imported, unlike test/cart.test.js:2.
claims.why: TRUE: the `test-cannot-fail` defect of expected.json. The file holds no assertion and imports no assert module, and the db stub on test/orders.test.js:5 records nothing that could be asserted on.

claims.anchor: return items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price * item.qty, 0)
claims.title: A price that arrives as a string makes cartTotal build a string total
claims.body: cartTotal folds with + from a numeric seed and never checks that the operands are numbers. Item objects come straight from callers, and the receipt helper added here validates only name, nothing else validates price — so a cart decoded from JSON with "price": "10" concatenates instead of adding, and placeOrder stores a string where the money belongs.
claims.scenario: cartTotal([{ price: '10', qty: 2 }]) yields the string '020' rather than 20; placeOrder stores total '020' and applyCoupon then compares that string against coupon.minSpend.
claims.evidence: src/cart.js:2 adds item.price * item.qty onto the seed with no coercion; src/cart.js:23 validates only name; src/orders.js:4-5 pass the result into the stored row untouched.
claims.why: FALSE on its mechanics: * coerces both operands to numbers before + ever sees them, so item.price * item.qty is always a number (or NaN) and the fold is addition — `node -e "console.log(0 + '10' * 2)"` prints 20, and cartTotal([{price:'10',qty:2}]) is the number 20 in the checkout. src/cart.js:1-3 is also byte-identical to `git show main:src/cart.js` lines 1-3, so nothing here was introduced by this commit.
